title: The Essence of Hayao Miyazaki Films: A Short Documentary About the Humanity at the Heart of His Animation
description:
in Animation, Creativity, Writing |   	July 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Film­mak­er Hayao Miyaza­ki detests being referred to as the Japan
body:
in Animation, Creativity, Writing |   	July 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Film­mak­er Hayao Miyaza­ki detests being referred to as the Japan­ese Walt Dis­ney. The great ani­ma­tor and sto­ry­teller admires the gor­geous ani­ma­tion of clas­sic Dis­ney films, but finds them lack­ing in emo­tion­al com­plex­i­ty, the ele­ment he prizes above all else.
Miyaza­k­i’s films are cel­e­brat­ed for their mys­ti­cal, super­nat­ur­al ele­ments, but they take shape around the human char­ac­ters inhab­it­ing them. Plot comes lat­er, after he has fig­ured out the desires dri­ving his peo­ple. “Keep it sim­ple,” he coun­sels in Lewis Bond’s short doc­u­men­tary The Essence of Human­i­ty above. An inter­est­ing piece of advice, giv­en that a hall­mark of his 60-year career is his insis­tence on cre­at­ing real­is­tic three-dimen­sion­al char­ac­ters, warts and all.
Amer­i­can ani­ma­tors are also taught to sim­pli­fy. They should all be able to sum up the essence of their pro­posed fea­tures by fill­ing in the blank of the phrase “I want _____,” pre­sum­ably because such con­ci­sion is a nec­es­sary ele­ment of a suc­cess­ful ele­va­tor pitch.
As Bond points out, West­ern ani­mat­ed fea­tures often end with a con­ve­nient deus ex machi­na, free­ing the char­ac­ters up for a crowd-pleas­ing dance par­ty as the cred­its roll.
Miyaza­ki doesn’t cot­ton to the idea of tidy, unearned end­ings, nor does he feel bound to grant his char­ac­ters their wants, pre­fer­ring instead to give them what they need. Spir­i­tu­al growth is supe­ri­or to wish ful­fill­ment here.
Such growth rarely hap­pens with­out time for reflec­tion, and Miyaza­ki films are notable for the num­ber of non-ver­bal scenes where­in char­ac­ters per­form small, every­day actions, a num­ber of which can be sam­pled in Bond’s doc­u­men­tary. The beau­ti­ful­ly ren­dered weath­er and set­tings have pro­vid­ed clues as to the char­ac­ters’ devel­op­ment, ever since the love­ly scene of cloud shad­ows skim­ming across a field in his first fea­ture, 1979’s The Cas­tle of Cagliostro.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2015.

Ayun Hal­l­i­day is an author, illus­tra­tor, and the­ater mak­er in NYC.

title: Christopher Nolan Picks 15 Favorite Films from the Criterion Closet
description:
in Film |   	July 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Maybe you’ve already seen Christo­pher Nolan’s new cin­e­mat­ic inter­pre­ta­tion of the Ody
body:
in Film |   	July 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Maybe you’ve already seen Christo­pher Nolan’s new cin­e­mat­ic inter­pre­ta­tion of the Odyssey more than once; maybe you don’t know whether you’ll ever get around to it at all. Either way, you’ve got to admit that the man makes films in a way very few liv­ing direc­tors do. His com­bi­na­tion of block­buster-scale spec­ta­cle and per­son­al vision, a rare expe­ri­ence indeed at the the­ater these days, can real­ly only be achieved by film­mak­ers with a thor­ough­go­ing love of the medi­um. Most of us will require no fur­ther proof of that love than this new video cap­tur­ing his vis­it to the Cri­te­ri­on Clos­et, that both hal­lowed and much-YouTubed space jam-packed with releas­es from the most wide­ly known home-video brand for cinephiles.
Unsur­pris­ing­ly, it’s not his first vis­it. “Last time I was here, there were no cam­eras, and I got to just come and steal some films,” he says, “but now I’m singing for my sup­per.” Unlike some film­mak­ers, he does­n’t play it cool for the audi­ence; rather, he imme­di­ate­ly starts pulling down Don Siegel’s neo-noir Hem­ing­way adap­ta­tion The Killers, a five-pic­ture John Cas­savetes box set, and Al Rein­ert’s Bri­an Eno-scored NASA doc­u­men­tary For All Mankind. It’s not a sur­prise to see him go for an Orson Welles movie, but the one that first catch­es his eye is Mr. Arkadin, which Welles “made all over the world in the scrap­pi­est, most sort of home­made, put-his-friends-togeth­er, grab-some-cos­tumes, find-an-inter­est­ing-loca­tion kind of way.”
Fritz Lang’s The Tes­ta­ment of Dr. Mabuse, he recalls, pro­vid­ed him and his broth­er-col­lab­o­ra­tor inspi­ra­tion for the Jok­er as famous­ly por­trayed by Heath Ledger in The Dark Knight. The com­plete Apu tril­o­gy by Satya­jit Ray reminds him that, how­ev­er great an impact the first of those films made on him, he nev­er did watch the oth­er two. For many movie­go­ers in the Eng­lish-speak­ing world of the mid-twen­ti­eth cen­tu­ry, Ray’s work was some of the first “world cin­e­ma” they’d ever seen; Nolan’s fel­low cinephile-auteur Mar­tin Scors­ese has done his part to bol­ster that tra­di­tion with his World Cin­e­ma Project series, and Nolan pulls off the shelf one of its vol­umes fea­tur­ing pic­tures from Cuba, Indone­sia, Iran, and else­where.
Though tech­ni­cal­ly British, Nolan is the par­tial­ly Chica­go-raised son of an Amer­i­can moth­er long since accept­ed as a kind of Hol­ly­wood native. His taste in movies, too, reflects a streak of high Amer­i­can­ism, which man­i­fests in selec­tions like Spike Lee’s Mal­colm X, David Lynch’s Lost High­way, Carl Franklin’s One False Move, and Richard Lin­klater’s Boy­hood. (As for Robert Alt­man’s satir­i­cal thriller The Play­er, it would be hard to imag­ine how he could­n’t appre­ci­ate its wicked­ly inci­sive depic­tion of “the Indus­try.”) Com­ing to the end of his Clos­et time, he also man­ages to grab God­frey Reg­gio’s Qat­si tril­o­gy, which con­sti­tutes “one of the great pieces of pure cin­e­ma,” and Car­roll Bal­lard’s The Black Stal­lion, a child­hood favorite that stayed with him. Like all the most suc­cess­ful film­mak­ers, Nolan under­stands that you’ve got to end strong, and in a way that does­n’t require expla­na­tion: hence, per­haps, his final choice of Cit­i­zen Kane.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: 'Colorstruck!' Examines the Connection Between Race and Chromatic Expression
description: A nude Black woman lies on a stark white chaise, her head propped up by her thin arm. She’s surrounded by flat, abstracted color in the form of fr
body:
A nude Black woman lies on a stark white chaise, her head propped up by her thin arm. She’s surrounded by flat, abstracted color in the form of fruits and fabrics, and a glass coupe and bottle on a nearby table offer a clear, rather than refracted, view of the vibrant scene. Rendered in oil on burlap, the painting by William H. Johnson is commanding in its palette and subject matter and an exemplary work in a new book by art historian Richard J. Powell.
Forthcoming this fall from Princeton University Press, Colorstruck! Painting, Pigment, Affect delves into the ways that color and social, political, and cultural forces intersect in Black American art. Powell takes an expansive approach to each of the three topics—painting, pigment, and affect—and examines works by a wide group of artists, including Jacob Lawrence, Alma Thomas, Lorna Simpson, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Nina Chanel Abney. His interest is in the dynamic interplay of paint and pigment and what the two reveal about both the artists and the viewers.
William H. Johnson, “Nude” (c. 1939), oil on burlap, 29 ¾ x 38 ¼ inches. Image courtesy of Smithsonian American Art Museum and Art Resource
Sharing a root with words like awestruck or starstruck, colorstruck is a slang term that evolved from “a Black person who preferred associating with light-skinned Blacks or White people to anyone inordinately preoccupied with race,” Powell writes. The idea is largely associated with colorism, although in his view, it can also be applied to the ways we marvel at and can even be overwhelmingly affected by an artist’s palette. He adds: 

What if a painter, like early Black modernist Willian H. Johnson, set aside the more pejorative insinuations in the idea of being colorstruck, and instead used the paint medium, an intense color palette, racial Blackness, and most important, his abstracting inclinations to produce an expressionistic, evocative, and disruptive work of art? 

The book continues in this line of thinking as it connects what is often thought of as a universal concept—that color exists, and humans respond to certain hues in particular ways—and the distinct context of race in America. Richly illustrated with archival photographs and numerous artworks, the volume captures the relationship between the unique experience of an artist and her viewer and the broader powers that inform those dynamics.
Colorstruck! Painting, Pigment, Affect will be published in September, and you can pre-order your copy through Bookshop.
Hervé Télémaque, “Négrerie (Black cultural effects)” (1974), lithograph, 30 x 22 inches. Image © The Metropolitan Museum of Art, courtesy of Art Resource
Alma Thomas, “The Eclipse” (1970), acrylic on canvas, 62 x 49 ¾ inches. Image courtesy of Smithsonian American Art Museum and Art Resource
Malcolm Bailey, “Untitled” (1972), cut and pasted paper and acrylic on Plexiglas, 36 x 36 inches. Image copyright © The Metropolitan Museum of Art, courtesy of Art Resource
Charles Alston, “Girl in a Red Dress” (1934), oil on canvas, 28 x 22 inches. Image © The Metropolitan Museum of Art, courtesy of Art Resource

title: Dynamic Scenes Emerge from Fumiaki Aono's Wooden Assemblages
description: Since 1998, Fumiaki Aono has been interested in how objects circulate and what happens when they appear in new contexts. Questions of restoration
body:
Since 1998, Fumiaki Aono has been interested in how objects circulate and what happens when they appear in new contexts. Questions of restoration and regeneration naturally followed, and wood became a prime medium for exploring these themes.
Today, Aono continues to revitalize found objects, particularly discarded furniture. Dressers, chests, and cabinets stack into towering assemblages and become the imaginative backdrop for the artist’s constructed scenes. Converted drawers appear like apartment buildings on a summer day, with tenants leaning out windows and hanging out at street level. Several works also depict box trucks and other vehicles emerging from wooden furnishings, while bicycles, hats, and shoes jut from the edges of sculptures to convey a sense of movement and evolution.

After experimenting with plywood and timber, Aono’s transition to secondhand furniture added a conceptual layer to the pieces. These objects “brought the old memories and lived histories of people into the imagery of the work. In recent years, my concept of ‘regeneration’ has evolved beyond mere physical form; it has become a highly complex and multifaceted process encompassing history, memory, ancient legends, and the deep psyche,” he says.
Explore more from the artist on his website and Instagram.

title: Betye Saar, Who Opened Portals Between Worlds, Dies at 99
body:
Obituary
                Her visionary assemblages recast the debris of American history into monuments of Black resilience and liberation.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Betye Saar in Los Angeles (2026) (photo David Sprague, courtesy Roberts Projects)
    
        
            Betye Saar, who trawled the depraved archive of Americana and transmuted its most vile depictions of Blackness into conceptually freighted assemblages that are mystical, moving, and revolutionary, died at 99 in Los Angeles yesterday, July 26. Her death was confirmed by Roberts Projects, which represented her.

title: An Exhibition Lets Self-Taught Artists Speak for Themselves
description:
Art Review
                 At the Folk Art Museum, “Self-Made” overcomes the problem of “insiders” ventriloquizing self-taught
body:
Art Review
                 At the Folk Art Museum, “Self-Made” overcomes the problem of “insiders” ventriloquizing self-taught artists.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Joe Coleman, "Voyage to Candyland" (2026), acrylic on panel (© Joe Coleman; photo Adam Reich, courtesy the American Folk Art Museum; all other photos Ekin Erkan/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            It should come as no surprise that the term “outsider art” was coined not by any of the artists it applies to but by an “insider” academic, Roger Cardinal, in 1972. This explains why the concept was limited to late 19th and early 20th-century “Sunday painters" like Henri Rousseau, William Doriani, and Morris Hirshfield rather than any of the preceding millennia of artists. Museums, too, have played a role in limiting how “outsider art” has been traditionally understood. Collectors and curators like Jean and Howard Lipman helped introduce European-American self-taught artists into the collections of North American art institutions like the Whitney and High Museums during the mid-20th century. But in doing so, they often overlooked myriad traditions — including ones that were geographically proximate, like Haudenosaunee art or Hopi Kachina carving.

title: The Smithsonian Is Not the President's Museum
description:
Opinion
                The Trump administration’s latest order marks an unprecedented effort to subordinate one of America's fo
body:
Opinion
                The Trump administration’s latest order marks an unprecedented effort to subordinate one of America's foremost public institutions to partisan power.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Members of the U.S. Park Police guard an entrance to the 9th Street tunnel in front of the Smithsonian Arts + Industries Building on August 13, 2025 in Washington, DC. (photo Alex Wong/Getty Images)
    
        
            In 1846, the Smithsonian Institution was established, in the words of its benefactor and namesake, British scientist James Smithson, “for the increase & diffusion of Knowledge among men.” Today, the 21 museums centered in Washington, DC, and more than 200 affiliates throughout the United States, have indeed increased and diffused knowledge in the maintenance of an astounding 157 million objects. Along with the preservation and distribution of knowledge — never a neutral term — these museums have been the site of discourse and debate, conversation and controversy, as any indispensable cultural institution should be. Over their long history, museums have “evolved to become institutions in which objects and learning are associated to help human beings understand the world around them,” writes John E. Simmons in Museums: A History (2022). Even while such institutions have always bolstered official narratives and aggrandized governments, in an ostensibly democratic country, the Smithsonian has embodied Simmons’s observation with its legacy of being administered in a spirit of expertise rather than just by politics. During its nearly two-century history, the Smithsonian has had its share of controversies, especially during the recent battle of attrition that is the Culture Wars. Right-wing critics accused the 1991 exhibition The West as America, Reinterpreting Images of the Frontier, 1820-1920 at the Smithsonian American Art Museum of being anti-American. A 1995 exhibition at the National Air and Space Museum about the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, which included the actual Enola Gay B-29 bomber that dropped the atomic bomb, drew criticism from veterans’ groups. Hide/Seek: Difference and Desire in American Portraiture, a 2010 exhibition of LGBTQ+ artists at the National Portrait Gallery, was denounced by conservatives as being “anti-Christian” because of a video art piece that featured 10 seconds of ants crawling on a crucifix. In all of these instances, the predictable occurred: Republican politicians fulminated and threatened to cancel federal funding, reactionary pundits bloviated and encouraged protest, and public debates (sometimes healthy and sometimes not) were waged around what the function of a museum should be. To varying degrees, such responses, and the responses to those responses, are expected markers of the discourse that defines democracy — though all of those exhibitions admirably served the institution’s original purpose outlined by Smithson. Demonstrators protesting against Trump’s executive actions aimed at the Smithsonian institution on May 3, 2025, in Washington, DC (photo by Craig Hudson/Washington Post via Getty Images)Last Friday, however, the Culture Wars escalated in an ominous fashion when the Trump administration issued an executive order with the loaded title “Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution.” The Secretary of the Interior, the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, the Administrator of General Services, and the Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy, it decreed, are now charged with installing “temporary signage along the [National Park Service]-maintained sidewalks and walkways used by the public to access the [National Museum of American History],” informing visitors of what the Executive Order terms “Ideological Capture.”
